newsitem.title: CAMEROON: Cameroon English speakers want to vote, not revolt.
newsitem.headline: Cameroon English speakers want to vote, not revolt.

text.p: Weeks after a spate of attacks by separatist gunmen, Cameroon's English-speaking opposition heartland is busy preparing for parliamentary elections -- not for insurrection.
Saturday's elections will be the second parliamentary poll since a return to multi-party politics in 1990 in the largely French-speaking Central African country.

"It is all a government ploy to prevent the holding of normal elections in the province," John Fru Ndi, leader of the Social Democratic Front (SDF) told Reuters in an interview, dismissing the attacks.

"We are sure to get an absolute majority in parliament. That will give us the power to change the constitution. Through a referendum Cameroonians will decide if they want a federation of two, four or 10 states," Fru Ndi said.
Unlike the more radical, Southern Cameroon National Council (SCNC), Fru Ndi's party is against total independence of the English-speaking part of the country.
Ordinary people seem to agree. "I have to vote normally and have peace afterwards. Nobody wants trouble in Bamenda, most people here do not feel threatened any more," said a librarian.

London-based human rights group Amnesty International has warned of human rights violations in the poll run-up, particularly in the Anglophone North-West province. It has called on President Paul Biya to ensure fair elections.
Bamenda, the main town, and the rest of the province have been under overnight curfew since March 30, although the curfew has been eased and now starts at 10 p.m. instead of dusk.

"I don't think that the curfew is affecting campaigning. It does affect the economy. But we would rather that the economy suffered a bit if it means security," said Egbe Enow, Secretary-General at the provincial governor's office.
Outside his office a truck is loaded with election material for the province's 10,487 polling stations. "We are preparing the elections with a lot of serenity," he said.
Police, gendarmes and troops remain deployed in the province, notably around the six localities where public buildings and police posts were attacked in March.
Local papers speak of army brutality in remote areas but the reports could not be independently confirmed.
In Bamenda, few army uniforms are in evidence and there is only one road-block on the road into town.
The Southern Cameroon National Council, a radical group mixing revolutionary rhetoric and a brand of religious fanaticism, has been calling since 1995 for secession by force.
Investigators say pictures and documents suggest its armed wing may have been behind the attacks.

"We are still investigating. So far we have arrested 12 people who have admitted that they were part of a seperatist commando group of about 24," Colonel Gomse Ousseini, commander of the para-military Gendarmerie, told Reuters.

Many opposition parties boycotted the last parliamentary poll in 1992. Biya's ruling Cameroon People's Democratic Rally (RDPC) emerged with 88 out of 180 seats in the national assembly. It formed an alliance with the small Movement for the Defence of the Republic (MDR) to ensure a majority.
This time 45 parties will field 1,800 candidates.
The SDF hopes to win at least 16 of the 20 North-West Province seats on Saturday.
